classification.difficultyReason: Uses the same routine linked derivative, root-sum/product and quadratic-formula decisions; the negative supplied root changes arithmetic rather than conceptual demand.

content.prompt: Consider the polynomial equation $x^4-x^3-13x^2-8x+12=0$. Show that $x=-2$ is a double root of the equation. Hence solve the equation.

answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^4-x^3-13x^2-8x+12$.
$$\begin{align*}P(-2)&=16+8-52+16+12=0\\P'(x)&=4x^3-3x^2-26x-8\\P'(-2)&=-32-12+52-8=0\\P''(x)&=12x^2-6x-26\\P''(-2)&=48+12-26=34\ne0\end{align*}$$
Therefore $x=-2$ has multiplicity exactly $2$. Let the remaining roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Using the sum and product of the four roots:
$$\begin{align*}-2-2+\alpha+\beta&=1\\\alpha+\beta&=5\\(-2)\times(-2)\times\alpha\beta&=12\\\alpha\beta&=3\end{align*}$$
The remaining roots satisfy
$$\begin{align*}x^2-5x+3&=0\\x&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{25-12}}2\\x&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{13}}2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=-2$ (double root), $\dfrac{5+\sqrt{13}}2$ or $\dfrac{5-\sqrt{13}}2$.
